---
title: "Metagame, Time Use, and Player Development in Online Chess: A Large-Scale Study of Lichess Games"
author: "Camden Bergquist"
date: "Last compiled on `r format(Sys.time(), '%B %d, %Y')`"
abstract: >
  Metagame change, time management, and player development are central but often separately studied dimensions of online chess behavior. Using 24 months of public Lichess data from January 2024 through December 2025, this study builds a reproducible large-scale pipeline that samples rated games and derives linked datasets for metagame composition, opening repertoire, time use, and longitudinal player outcomes. The analysis is observational and non-causal, combining descriptive modeling, multinomial opening models, player fixed-effects progression models, and clustering-based behavioral profiling with forward-in-time evaluation. Results indicate that the opening environment gradually spreads across a wider set of choices over time, although the extent of that spread differs by time control. Opening preferences also shift with skill, as stronger players devote a smaller share of games to the most common named openings. Patterns of time use vary by format: Higher-rated players move faster in blitz, think longer in rapid and classical, and enter low-time situations more often across all formats. In models of within-player change, later rating gains are associated more consistently with richer and less static opening repertoires and with more complex games than with sheer game volume. Clustering results likewise suggest that chess behavior is better understood as a set of recurring play states than as a small number of fixed player types. Together, these findings suggest that online chess improvement is associated less with sheer volume of play than with the quality and adaptability of engagement, while time-use patterns separately show that players manage pace and pressure in format-specific ways. More broadly, the results show how large-scale game logs can be used to study adaptation and skill development in online chess environments.

## Introduction

Competitive games have become an important source of large-scale behavioral data, enabling researchers to study strategic decision-making, skill development, and population-level trends using observational logs at scales rarely achievable in controlled studies [@edelmann2020css; @watts2014css]. Chess is one of the most-played competitive games in the world, and the relatively recent growth of online platforms has created datasets with millions to billions of games played under standardized rules and well-defined competitive contexts (e.g., time controls, ratings, game outcomes) [@watts2014css; @lichessDatabase]. One of the most widely used sources is the Lichess Open Database, which provides public monthly exports of rated games played on lichess.org in PGN format [@lichessDatabase; @lichessDatabaseGitHub]. These exports make it possible to study the ways strategy and performance vary across skill levels and time controls in a modern, online environment.

This study uses Lichess game data to investigate contemporary metagame behavior and player development. Here, 'metagame' refers to the population-level distribution of strategic choices and styles observed in practice – such as opening families, risk preferences, and game outcomes – within a defined time window and player population. In addition to describing how strategic behavior differs by rating and time control, we attempt to connect these strategic signatures to measures of player progression over time. Because online chess is a repeatedly played competitive setting with a mature rating infrastructure, it offers a natural testbed for quantifying skill and comparing behavior across a large player population [@lichessRatingSystems; @glickmanGlicko2Desc].

A central component of modern chess analytics is the rating system used to summarize player strength. The Elo rating system, originally developed for chess, models player performance probabilistically, and remains a foundational reference point for interpreting skill differences and expected outcomes in competitive settings [@elo1978rating; @fideElo2025]. Lichess uses a modified version of this system called 'Glicko-2', which, in addition to rating, tracks uncertainty via rating deviation and volatility [@lichessRatingSystems; @glickmanGlicko2Desc]. Skill ratings are especially useful for observational studies like this one because they provide a consistent scale by which to stratify players and construct longitudinal measures of improvement [@glickmanGlicko2Desc].

Overall, this project brings together data science, computational social science, and strategic-behavior research by treating online chess as a real-world environment in which strategic choices and performance outcomes can be measured at scale and analyzed using statistical learning methods [@edelmann2020css; @watts2014css].

### Background {#sec-background}

A growing research literature uses large online chess datasets to study human performance, decision-making, and strategic patterns. For example, Chowdhary et al. use an online chess dataset of more than 100 million games to quantify performance dynamics and career-like trajectories, illustrating how large game archives support population-level behavioral measurement across skill levels [@chowdhary2023performance].

One important line of work focuses on time usage and decision quality under time constraints. Online chess platforms record both move sequences and clock information, which allows researchers to study how players allocate thinking time and how time pressure shapes decisions. Russek et al. analyze millions of Lichess games to relate move times to the estimated value of additional computation, and show that time allocation patterns vary systematically with playing strength and time control [@russek2025thinking]. These findings support the idea that online chess is a rich setting for studying bounded rationality and performance under constraints, especially when comparing bullet, blitz, rapid, and classical formats [@russek2025thinking].

Chess opening choice is also an active research topic. Because openings are discrete, labelable strategic choices that occur early in every game, they are well suited to population-level analysis. De Marzo and Servedio use online chess community data to quantify opening similarity and complexity, including representing openings in network form and studying how opening-related structure can be used to forecast future opening adoption [@demarzo2023openings]. This motivates analyzing metagame development in terms of shifting opening popularity and success rates across time, player skill, and time controls [@demarzo2023openings; @chowdhary2023performance].

Finally, there is an emerging interest in identifying player styles or archetypes from game logs. While traditional chess analysis often focuses on engine evaluation of positions, a complementary approach is to extract behavioral features from move sequences and outcomes (e.g., game length, opening selection, and other style proxies) and use statistical learning to characterize player types. For instance, McIlroy-Young et al. demonstrate that models trained on move sequences can capture individual-specific signatures ('style') in player decisions, supporting the notion that player behavior is meaningfully distinguishable from game records alone [@mcilroyyoung2021stylometry]. This creates a bridge between strategic analysis (what players choose to do) and longitudinal outcomes (how players improve or persist over time).

Collectively, existing work suggests that large-scale online chess datasets support three relevant kinds of analysis: (1) descriptive metagame analysis of strategic choices across populations; (2) modeling the way constraints (such as time pressure) affect behavior and outcomes; and (3) data-driven modeling of player growth and characterization of potential player types [@chowdhary2023performance; @russek2025thinking; @demarzo2023openings; @mcilroyyoung2021stylometry]. Here, we build on those themes by using Lichess data to analyze contemporary opening and style patterns and relate them to measures of player performance and development over time.

## The Data {#sec-data}

### Source {#sec-source}

Lichess is the largest open-source chess server in the world and releases free monthly exports of its game data under the Creative Commons CC0 license [@lichessDatabase]. The site logs game data while a game is being played, and allows users to retroactively analyze both the games they have played and those of others on the platform. Although Lichess offers a powerful API, we elected to download data directly from their website in `.pgn.zst` format. The PGN (portable game notation) format is a plaintext format for chess games, containing moves, metadata headers (e.g., players, date, and event), and optional annotation. The `.zst` file extension denotes Zstandard compression, a modern compression format commonly used for its speed and efficiency. In practice, Zstandard substantially reduces the storage required for large PGN archives.

For the purposes of this study, we downloaded 24 months of Lichess game data spanning from January 2024 to December 2025, amounting to approximately 677 gigabytes of raw data when compressed. This volume – nearly 700 gigabytes compressed, or roughly 3–4 terabytes uncompressed – was too large to process conveniently on local hardware alone. We therefore relied on a hybrid R/Python pipeline that downloads the data, deterministically samples and parses it into partitioned parquet files, and then constructs smaller analysis-ready datasets from those outputs.

The download and parsing section of the pipeline performs the following:

- Reads a config file `pipeline.yml` that controls the scope and parameters of the pipeline's operation.
- Downloads monthly Lichess 'standard rated' PGN archives for each month specified in the YAML.
- Decompresses each Zstandard file as a stream, scanning games one-by-one to prevent memory bottlenecks.
- Parses game headers first to determine whether a game meets the sampling and filtering criteria before doing more expensive parsing work.
  - Extracts core metadata (players, ratings, time control, result, termination, opening, timestamps).
  - Buckets each game into blitz/rapid/classical using a Lichess-style estimated-duration rule based on $\text{initial} + 40 \times \text{increment}$ seconds.
- Applies filtering rules from the YAML, which in this case are:
  - Include only blitz/rapid/classical time controls.
  - Include only games from players in the 800–2600 rating range.
  - Drop unwanted terminations (aborted games).
- Uses deterministic hash-based sampling to create reproducible subsets without needing to store the whole population:
  - A meta sample keyed by `game_id` for population/metagame summaries, at a rate of 5/500 games.
  - A player cohort keyed by `username` for longitudinal/player tracking at a rate of 3/500 players.
  - A moves sample keyed by `game_id` for clock/time-per-move data at a rate of 5/10000 moves.
- Deterministically anonymizes usernames based on a stable, salted hash.
  - Cohort selection is computed on the real username before anonymization, so it remains reproducible.
- Writes month-partitioned parquet outputs for game-level data.

The dataset-building portion of the pipeline takes those outputs and, using DuckDB to read and write parquet files on disk, builds seven datasets from them:

- Player-level longitudinal summary tables from `games_cohort`:
  - `player_month` (`pm`): $\text{player} \times \text{month}$, 249,761 observations.
  - `player_month_tc` (`pm_tc`): $\text{player} \times \text{month} \times \text{time control}$, 320,869 observations.
- Player-opening 'repertoire' table from `games_cohort`:
  - `player_opening_month_tc` (`pom_tc`): $\text{player} \times \text{month} \times \text{time control} \times \text{opening}$, 7,167,580 observations.
- Metagame tables from `games_meta`:
  - `meta_opening_month_tc` (`mom_tc`): $\text{openings} \times \text{month} \times \text{time control}$, 130,672 observations.
  - `meta_month_tc` (`mm_tc`): $\text{month} \times \text{time control}$, 72 observations.
- Time-usage tables from `moves_meta`:
  - `player_time_month_tc` (`ptm_tc`): $\text{player} \times \text{month} \times \text{time control}$, 1,038,050 observations.
  - `moves_month_tc` (`mvm_tc`): $\text{month} \times \text{time control}$, 72 observations.

The pipeline logs session and version info for both R and Python and records checksums for downloaded raw files to help with reproducibility.

### Variables

The analysis uses several linked derived datasets rather than a single analytic table. In all cases, the raw unit of data is a rated chess game from the Lichess public database, but the pipeline aggregates games and sometimes moves into analysis-ready summaries. At the player level, `pm` and `pm_tc` summarize monthly outcomes overall and by time control; `pom_tc` captures opening use within player-month-time-control cells; `ptm_tc` summarizes move-time behavior; and `mom_tc` and `mm_tc` provide population-level metagame summaries. Because these tables operate at different units of analysis, the main text introduces them only at the level needed for later modeling. Full variable definitions are reported in Appendix [-@sec-appendix-a].

Together, these analytical levels support longitudinal player-performance modeling (`pm`, `pm_tc`), repertoire and style measurement from opening choice (`pom_tc`), metagame analysis via opening adoption and outcomes (`mom_tc`), and time-management analysis using move-time features (`ptm_tc`).^[The remaining tables, `mm_tc` and `mvm_tc`, are summary-level datasets used mainly for aggregate diagnostics and macro-level summaries rather than player-level modeling.]


### Cleaning

Most cleaning steps were performed during the pipeline’s parsing stage. Additional standardization and feature construction steps not covered in @sec-source include:

- `TimeControl` tag parsed into:
  - `initial` (seconds).
  - `increment` (seconds).
  - `tc_bucket`, based on estimated duration $\text{initial} + 40 \times \text{increment}$ seconds:
    - `< 180 = bullet`, `< 600 = blitz`, `< 1800 = rapid`, else `classical`.
- Converted PGN result strings into:
  - `winner` (white/black/draw).
  - `score_white` (1/0.5/0).
- Computed upset indicators using ratings:
  - `rating_diff` = `white_rating` - `black_rating`.
  - `abs_rating_diff`
  - `is_upset`
- Computed game length in `moves` from move sequences for use in the derived datasets.

The resulting data were then restructured and aggregated into tidy analysis tables.

## Exploratory Data Analysis {#sec-eda}

This section summarizes the main descriptive patterns in the sampled data before formal modeling. It first documents support and reliability constraints that affect interpretation, then turns to broad patterns in opening behavior and time usage. Full supporting diagnostics are reported in Appendix [-@sec-appendix-b].

### Coverage and Reliability{#sec-eda-coverage}

Before turning to observed patterns, it is useful to clarify which parts of the sampled data are more and less strongly supported. @fig-coverage shows that the number of observations differs substantially across time controls, with blitz appearing more often than rapid, and both appearing much more often than classical. This is a direct consequence of our parsing method: The pipeline sampled from the underlying game population rather than enforcing balanced coverage by format. As such, the cleaned data preserve the activity structure of the platform itself. That is not a problem in its own right, but it does mean that comparisons across time controls come with unequal precision, especially where classical is concerned.


```{r Coverage Plot}
#| label: fig-coverage
#| fig-cap: "Coverage of player-month-time-control observations over time by time control."
#| fig-align: center

cov_pm_tc <- dbGetQuery(con, sprintf("
  SELECT month, tc_bucket, COUNT(*) AS n_rows
  FROM read_parquet(%s)
  GROUP BY month, tc_bucket
  ORDER BY month, tc_bucket
", qpath(paths$pm_tc))) |>
  mutate(
    month_date = as.Date(paste0(month, "-01")),
    tc_bucket = factor(
      tc_bucket,
      levels = c("blitz", "rapid", "classical")
    )
  )

ggplot(cov_pm_tc, aes(x = month_date, y = n_rows, group = tc_bucket, color = tc_bucket)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  labs(x = "Month", y = "Observations", color = "Time Control") +
  scale_x_date(
    breaks = as.Date(c("2024-03-01", "2024-06-01", "2024-09-01", "2024-12-01", "2025-03-01", "2025-06-01", "2025-09-01", "2025-12-01")),
    date_labels = "%Y-%m"
  ) +
  scale_color_few(
    labels = c("Blitz", "Rapid", "Classical")
  ) +
  theme_few() + 
  theme(
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(linewidth = 0.3, colour = "grey85"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )
```

A second limitation is that the player panel is unbalanced. @fig-panel-depth shows that many players appear for only a few months, while a much smaller subset remain observable across all or most of the two-year window. This pattern is expected in an online hobby setting, but it matters once the analysis shifts from cross-sectional summaries to player-level change over time. Any lagged or forward-looking quantity necessarily relies on re-observing the same player in later months, so longitudinal analyses operate on a smaller and more selective subset than the full sampled panel. 

```{r Panel Depth Plot}
#| label: fig-panel-depth
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of months observed per player in the sampled panel."
#| fig-align: center

panel_len <- dbGetQuery(con, sprintf("
  WITH x AS (
    SELECT player, COUNT(DISTINCT month) AS n_months
    FROM read_parquet(%s)
    GROUP BY player
  )
  SELECT n_months, COUNT(*) AS n_players
  FROM x
  GROUP BY n_months
  ORDER BY n_months
", qpath(paths$pm)))

ggplot(panel_len, aes(x = n_months, y = n_players)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue", color = "steelblue") +
  scale_y_continuous() +
  labs(x = "Months Observed per Player", y = "Players") +
  theme_few()
```

Overall, the data are informative but unevenly supported. Some parts of the sample are much better represented than others, so short-horizon player outcomes should be interpreted with appropriate caution. @sec-methodology and @sec-modeling address these issues more directly.


### Opening Behavior {#sec-eda-opening}

The opening plots suggest considerably more temporal stability than rapid metagame turnover. At the level of the most common named openings, there is not much evidence of dramatic month-to-month turnover across the two-year sample window; the basic impression is one of gradual change as opposed to rapid metagame cycling. Although the degree of stability differs by time control, the same broad pattern appears across all three formats. Additional time-control-specific plots are reported in Appendix [-@sec-appendix-b].


```{r Opening by Rating}
#| label: fig-opening-rating
#| fig-cap: "Opening share by rating for most common blitz openings."
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-height: 4

# Settings
tc_use <- "blitz"
bin_width <- 200
top_k <- 8 # Number of openings to plot
min_bin_total <- 2000 # Min player-games in a rating bin

# Pick top openings within tc_bucket (weighted by games)
top_openings <- dbGetQuery(con, sprintf("
  WITH x AS (
    SELECT opening, SUM(games) AS total_games
    FROM read_parquet(%s)
    WHERE tc_bucket = '%s'
      AND opening IS NOT NULL
    GROUP BY opening
  )
  SELECT opening
  FROM x
  ORDER BY total_games DESC
  LIMIT %d
", qpath(paths$pom_tc), tc_use, top_k))

open_list <- paste0(
  "('", paste(gsub("'", "''", top_openings$opening), collapse="','"), "')"
)

# Compute opening share within rating bins
trend_rating <- dbGetQuery(con, sprintf("
  WITH base AS (
    SELECT
      tc_bucket,
      opening,
      avg_rating,
      games
    FROM read_parquet(%s)
    WHERE tc_bucket = '%s'
      AND opening IN %s
      AND opening IS NOT NULL
      AND avg_rating IS NOT NULL
      AND games IS NOT NULL
  ),
  binned AS (
    SELECT
      opening,
      CAST(FLOOR(avg_rating / %d) * %d AS INTEGER) AS rating_bin_lo,
      SUM(games) AS player_games
    FROM base
    GROUP BY opening, rating_bin_lo
  ),
  totals AS (
    SELECT
      rating_bin_lo,
      SUM(player_games) AS bin_total
    FROM binned
    GROUP BY rating_bin_lo
  )
  SELECT
    b.rating_bin_lo,
    (b.rating_bin_lo + %d - 1) AS rating_bin_hi,
    b.opening,
    b.player_games,
    t.bin_total,
    CAST(b.player_games AS DOUBLE) / t.bin_total AS share
  FROM binned b
  JOIN totals t USING (rating_bin_lo)
  WHERE t.bin_total >= %d
  ORDER BY b.rating_bin_lo, b.opening
", qpath(paths$pom_tc), tc_use, open_list,
   bin_width, bin_width, bin_width, min_bin_total))


trend_rating <- trend_rating |>
  mutate(
    rating_bin = paste0(rating_bin_lo, "\u2013", rating_bin_hi),
    rating_bin = factor(rating_bin, levels = unique(rating_bin))
  )

ggplot(trend_rating, aes(x = rating_bin, y = share, color = opening, group = opening)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 0.1)) +
  labs(
    x = "Rating",
    y = "Share of Games",
    color = ""
  ) +
  scale_color_few(labels = function(x) str_wrap(x, width = 28)) +
  theme_few() +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(linewidth = 0.3, colour = "grey85"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle=60, hjust=1)
  ) + 
  guides(color = guide_legend(nrow = 4, byrow = TRUE))
```
@fig-opening-rating is more informative for interpretation. Although broad temporal drift appears fairly modest, opening share changes more clearly across rating levels. Some openings gain relative share as player rating increases, while others lose it, and those gradients are easier to see than the changes over calendar time. The Pirc Defense and Philidor Defense are especially good examples. Even where the shifts are not large in absolute terms, the rating structure is clearer than anything suggested by the over-time plots alone.

In summary, the exploratory evidence suggests that opening behavior is better framed as structured choice by rating and format, with gradual long-tail diversification, than as rapid turnover among named openings.

### Time Use {#sec-eda-time}

The time-usage plots show clearer structure. @fig-time shows a clear difference in thinking time across both time controls and skill levels. Blitz and classical show opposite gradients: Stronger players spend less time per move in blitz, but more time per move in classical. Rapid lies somewhere in between. Even without formal modeling, this shows that time control is not just a background element; it fundamentally changes the relationship between rating and pace.


```{r Time Use}
#| label: fig-time
#| fig-cap: "Average time spent per move by player rating and time control."
#| fig-align: center

time_bin <- dbGetQuery(con, sprintf("
  SELECT
    tc_bucket,
    floor(avg_rating/100)*100 AS rating_bin,
    AVG(avg_time_spent) AS mean_time_spent,
    SUM(move_rows) AS total_moves
  FROM read_parquet(%s)
  GROUP BY tc_bucket, rating_bin
  HAVING total_moves >= 20000
  ORDER BY tc_bucket, rating_bin
", qpath(paths$ptm_tc)))

time_bin$tc_bucket <- factor(
  time_bin$tc_bucket,
  levels = c("blitz", "rapid", "classical")
)

ggplot(time_bin, aes(x = rating_bin, y = mean_time_spent, color = tc_bucket, group = tc_bucket)) +
  geom_line() +
    facet_wrap(~factor(tc_bucket, levels = c("blitz", "rapid", "classical")), scales="free_y", labeller = as_labeller(c(
      blitz = "Blitz",
      rapid = "Rapid",
      classical = "Classical"
    ))) +
  labs(x = "Player Rating", y = "Average Time per Move (Seconds)") +
  scale_color_few() +
  theme_few() + 
  theme(
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(linewidth = 0.3, colour = "grey85"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "none"
  )
```

A useful supporting pattern is that the same broad structure remains visible when time use is broken down by game phase, suggesting that the broad time-use gradients in @fig-time are not just artifacts of averaging everything together. Appendix [-@sec-appendix-b] reports the corresponding phase-specific diagnostics. All in all, time management does not look one-dimensional. Average pace changes across formats, and the meaning of 'using more time' depends heavily on the time control in question, which makes time usage look like a genuine behavioral outcome rather than a mechanical byproduct of format alone.

## Methodology {#sec-methodology}

This section describes the analytic preparation, feature construction, and modeling framework used in the study. The analysis is observational and non-causal throughout; models are used for description, association, prediction, and exploratory summarization, *not* causal identification.

Because the project combines several research questions across multiple linked datasets, the methodology proceeds in two stages. First, variables are transformed and aligned so that quantities are comparable across players, months, and time controls. Second, we define a set of modeling tasks aligned with the project goals: metagame dynamics, opening popularity, time use, player progression, and player categorization.

All predictive modeling uses forward-in-time data splits. Training data are drawn from earlier months in the sample window, while validation and test data are drawn from later contiguous months. Splitting is performed at the month level so that observations from a given month are never used to predict themselves or earlier periods. This design reduces temporal leakage and makes held-out evaluation more realistic, especially for progression targets defined for future rating change. Where relevant, models are also checked across time-control and rating strata to ensure that conclusions are not driven by a single format or skill band.


### Data Transformations {#sec-methodology-transformations}

The linked analytic tables described in @sec-data operate at different observational units and therefore require additional alignment before modeling. Transformations were implemented to improve comparability across contexts, reduce instability in sparse cells, and construct interpretable predictors for the later analyses.

#### Analytic Alignment and Scaling {#sec-methodology-transformations-alignment}

The project does not rely on a single modeling table. Instead, different tasks use different analytic units, including player-month summaries, player-month-by-time-control summaries, opening-level repertoire tables, metagame month summaries, and move-time summaries. These tables were retained at their native units whenever possible so that each model could be fit on the level most appropriate to its target. As a result, some models operate on aggregate month-level data, while others operate on player-period or opening-period observations.

Rating was sometimes converted from a continuous quantity into bins for descriptive summaries, nonparametric plots, and models that benefited from coarse stratification. This was done primarily to stabilize estimates and improve interpretability in settings where fine-grained rating variation was not necessary. For clustering and other multivariate feature-based analyses, retained numeric inputs were standardized as z-scores so that variables measured on different scales – e.g., seconds, proportions, counts, rating points – would contribute on a comparable basis.

#### Weighting, Thresholds, and Support {#sec-methodology-transformations-weighting}

Many outcomes are rates or shares estimated from cells with unequal support. Some observations are based on large numbers of games or move rows, whereas others are based on very small samples and are correspondingly volatile. For this reason, weighting and support restrictions were used where appropriate.

When player-level quantities needed to be collapsed across time controls, overall summaries were constructed using exposure-based weighting. For example, overall player-month rating was computed as a games-weighted average of time-control-specific average ratings, and overall time-pressure quantities were computed using move-based weighting when derived from move-level summaries. This approach prevents low-volume cells from exerting the same influence as high-volume cells when constructing cross-format summaries.

Minimum-support thresholds were also applied in settings where extremely sparse observations would otherwise dominate. Depending on the task, these thresholds were defined in terms of games per player-month, games per opening cell, or move rows per time-use summary. These filters were not intended to alter the substantive population under study, but rather to limit the influence of cells whose estimates were too unstable to reliably interpret.

#### Derived Features and Missingness {#sec-methodology-transformations-derived}

Several interpretable features were constructed from the player-opening and time-use tables for use in the progression and categorization analyses. These features were intended to summarize broad aspects of player behavior.

Repertoire breadth was measured using opening diversity, defined as the number of distinct openings used within the relevant period. Repertoire concentration was summarized using the share of games allocated to the player’s most-used opening. Repertoire adjustment was captured in two related ways—  an indicator for whether the most-played opening changed from the previous month, and measures of month-to-month repertoire churn based on changes in opening-share vectors and the appearance of newly used openings. Time-use behavior was summarized using variables such as average time spent per move, upper-tail move-time summaries, opening-phase time allocation, and low-time frequency.^[Phase-specific time-use variables use move-count intervals rather than engine-defined phases: opening is moves 1--10, middlegame is moves 11--25, and endgame is moves 26 and later. Low-time definition: A move is flagged as "low time" if the remaining clock time after the move satisfies $\text{clock\_after} \le \max\!\left(10,\; 2 \times \text{increment}\right)$ seconds, where $\text{increment}$ is the per-move increment of the game's time control.]

Some time-use variables were structurally missing rather than randomly absent. In particular, endgame time measures are often unavailable because many games do not reach the move-number threshold used to define the endgame phase. These missing values therefore reflect game structure rather than arbitrary loss of data. Models using phase-specific variables either handled these cases explicitly or restricted analysis to observations for which the relevant phase was meaningfully defined.


### Modeling Tasks and Candidate Specifications {#sec-methodology-models}

Because this paper addresses several distinct questions, candidate models are organized by modeling task rather than abstract model family. Each task corresponds to a substantive question, a natural observational unit, and a set of candidate specifications suited to that problem. Formal model comparison and retention are deferred to @sec-modeling. The present section instead defines the role of each modeling task and the types of specifications considered.


#### Metagame Dynamics {#sec-metagame-dynamics}

Metagame-dynamics models were used to describe how aggregate ecosystem measures changed across month and time control. These models focus on population-level structure rather than individual players. Depending on the outcome, the primary observational units were either month-by-time-control summaries or opening-by-month-by-time-control summaries.

The main outcomes in this task include concentration and diversity measures, draw rate, upset rate, average game length, and opening share. Predictors primarily include month, time control, and their interactions. Candidate specifications included weighted linear models for macro outcomes and multinomial models for opening composition, with simpler opening-by-opening share models considered as descriptive comparisons.

The motivation for using more than one specification in this task is straightforward. Some metagame quantities, such as concentration or average moves, are scalar month-level summaries and are naturally modeled with weighted regressions. Opening composition, by contrast, is inherently compositional— increases in one opening’s share imply decreases elsewhere. Models that account for this compositional structure were therefore considered when the goal was to describe substitution within the opening ecosystem.


#### Opening Popularity {#sec-opening-popularity}

Opening-popularity models were used to describe how opening choice varied with player strength and time control. This task overlaps with metagame analysis but is narrower in scope; rather than modeling the ecosystem as a whole, it focuses specifically on opening-adoption patterns.

The primary observational unit for this task is the month-by-time-control-by-rating-bin opening summary. Outcomes are opening shares or opening-use counts, and the key predictors are rating level, time control, month, and rating-by-format interactions. Candidate specifications included pooled multinomial models as the main compositional approach, along with count-based and weighted share models as lower-complexity alternatives.

This task treats opening popularity as a structured choice problem. The multinomial framework is useful because it represents the full set of retained openings jointly, allowing probabilities to coherently shift across categories. Simpler single-opening models remain useful as descriptive checks, but fail to fully represent substitution across openings and as such play a secondary role in this modeling category.


#### Time Use {#sec-time-use}

Time-use models were used to characterize how time allocation varied across skill and time control. These models treat time management as a behavioral outcome rather than as a byproduct of format alone. Two related targets were emphasized— average time use and low-time frequency.

Depending on the target, the primary observational units were either player-month-by-time-control summaries or month-level time-use summaries. Outcomes include average time spent per move, upper-tail move-time summaries, phase-specific averages, and the proportion of moves taken in low-time states. The central predictors are player rating, time control, and in some cases their interaction, with month included where temporal adjustment is needed.

Candidate specifications included additive and interaction regressions for mean time-use outcomes, robust or quantile-based alternatives for heavy-tailed variables, and bounded-outcome models for low-time frequency. The reason for considering multiple mean-modeling strategies is that time-use data can be skewed and sensitive to outliers, while low-time frequency is both bounded and concentrated near zero. Different specifications were considered depending on whether the main challenge was nonlinearity, heavy tails, or bounded proportion structure.


#### Player Progression {#sec-player-progression}

Player-progression models were used to relate current-month behavior to later rating movement. These models ask whether within-player changes in activity, game structure, repertoire behavior, and related features are associated with subsequent changes in rating over short horizons.

The baseline observational unit is the player-month table, optionally joined to time-control or repertoire summaries when the required predictors are available. Outcomes are defined as future rating change over one- and three-month horizons, along with an absolute-change outcome used to summarize movement magnitude without direction. Predictors include current rating, game volume, average game length, repertoire breadth, repertoire concentration, repertoire adjustment, and selected time-use features where support permits.

Candidate specifications included regularized linear models, panel-data models, and tree-based regressions. Regularized models were considered because many player-level predictors are correlated. Panel models were considered because the data are longitudinal and repeated within players. Tree-based models were considered as flexible predictive benchmarks capable of capturing nonlinearities and interactions without extensive manual specification. Because this task is explicitly forward-looking, realistic temporal splitting is especially important; the model must predict later rating movement using only information available at the current month.


#### Player Categorization {#sec-player-categorization}

Player-categorization models were used to summarize recurring behavioral profiles in player-month observations. This task is exploratory rather than inferential. The goal is not to estimate latent causal types, but to determine whether broad behavioral configurations can be recovered from performance, repertoire, and activity features.

The natural observational unit is a joined player-month-by-time-control table containing performance measures, repertoire summaries, and other standardized features. Inputs include rating, rating differential, game length, outcome rates, repertoire breadth, repertoire concentration, repertoire adjustment, and selected activity measures. Time-use variables were considered where coverage allowed, but their inclusion depended on support in the merged sample.

Candidate specifications included dimensionality-reduction methods and clustering algorithms. Dimensionality reduction was used to summarize major axes of behavioral variation and to inspect whether lower-dimensional structure was visible in the data. Clustering methods were used to partition the feature space into interpretable behavioral groupings. Because the goal of this task is descriptive summarization, later evaluation emphasizes balance, stability, and interpretability rather than formal inference.


### Summary {#sec-methodology-summary}

Taken together, these transformations and modeling tasks define the analytic structure of the paper. The transformations align linked datasets, stabilize sparse quantities, and produce interpretable features for later use. The modeling tasks then organize the empirical questions into five domains: ecosystem-level metagame change, opening choice, time management, longitudinal progression, and exploratory behavioral profiling.

## Modeling {#sec-modeling}

This section compares the candidate models introduced in @sec-methodology-models and identifies the specifications retained for the remainder of the analysis. The purpose here is not to present substantive findings, but to narrow a broader set of candidate models to a smaller set of primary specifications for each modeling task. Substantive interpretation is deferred to @sec-results.

Model retention is based on four considerations: inferential suitability, held-out predictive adequacy, robustness to reasonable specification changes, and interpretability. These criteria do not apply identically to every modeling problem. In some cases, the retained model is primarily inferential; in others, it is better understood as descriptive or predictive. This distinction is especially important for exploratory methods such as clustering, which are useful for summarizing structure in the data but are not treated as a basis for inferential claims.

Because a large number of models were fit during development, the body of this section focuses on retention decisions and the reasons for them. Detailed predictive comparisons, robustness checks, and supplemental diagnostics are reported in Appendices [-@sec-appendix-c], [-@sec-appendix-d], [-@sec-appendix-e], and [-@sec-appendix-f].

### Metagame Dynamics {#sec-metagame-dynamics-2}

Metagame dynamics were modeled at two related levels. First, aggregate ecosystem and game-environment outcomes were modeled at the month-by-time-control level. These macro outcomes included opening concentration and diversity, along with draw rate, upset rate, and average moves. Second, opening composition itself was modeled separately by time control using specifications designed for compositional outcomes.

For the macro outcomes, weighted linear models were retained as the primary inferential framework. These specifications provided a direct and interpretable way to estimate time trends and time-control differences while accommodating unequal support across month-by-format cells. Because the macro series are observed over time, inference relied on heteroskedasticity- and autocorrelation-consistent standard errors.


```{=latex}
\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\caption{Retained macro metagame model.}
\label{fig:eq-metagame-macro}

\small
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
Y_{c,t}
&=
\beta_0
+
\beta_1 t
+
\beta_2\,\mathbf{1}\{c=\text{Classical}\}
+
\beta_3\,\mathbf{1}\{c=\text{Rapid}\} \\
&\quad
+
\beta_4\,t\,\mathbf{1}\{c=\text{Classical}\}
+
\beta_5\,t\,\mathbf{1}\{c=\text{Rapid}\}
+
\varepsilon_{c,t}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}

\par\medskip
\begin{minipage}{0.92\linewidth}
\footnotesize
Here, $Y_{c,t}$ denotes a month-by-time-control metagame outcome, such as HHI concentration, effective number of openings, draw rate, upset rate, or average moves. Blitz is the reference time-control category. Inference used Newey--West heteroskedasticity- and autocorrelation-consistent standard errors.
\end{minipage}

\end{figure}
```

Opening composition required a different retained model because opening shares are inherently compositional. Candidate models included weighted fixed-effects share regressions, GAM-based share regressions, and multinomial specifications fit separately by time control. The multinomial models were retained as the primary inferential basis for compositional change because they represent the full opening set jointly and therefore respect the substitution structure of opening shares. By contrast, the share-based alternatives model openings one at a time and are better treated as descriptive comparisons than as primary inferential models.

```{=latex}
\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\caption{Retained multinomial metagame-composition model, fit separately by time control.}
\label{fig:eq-metagame-multinomial}

\small
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(Y_t = k)
&=
\frac{\exp(\eta_{k,t})}
{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(\eta_{j,t})},
\quad k=1,\dots,K, \\
\eta_{k,t}
&=
\alpha_k + \beta_k t,
\quad k=1,\dots,K-1, \\
\eta_{K,t}
&=0.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}

\par\medskip
\begin{minipage}{0.92\linewidth}
\footnotesize
Here, $Y_t$ denotes the opening category at month $t$, and $k$ indexes the retained opening categories. The final category, $K$, is the reference category, so category-specific effects are interpreted relative to that baseline.
\end{minipage}

\end{figure}
```

Robustness checks further supported this division of labor. Changes to the retained opening set altered predictive difficulty in the expected way, but did not overturn the main directional patterns of the multinomial results. Detailed comparisons and robustness checks for both the macro and compositional models are reported in Appendix [-@sec-appendix-c].


### Opening Popularity {#sec-opening-popularity-2}

Opening popularity was modeled primarily as a compositional problem. The main inferential candidate was a pooled multinomial model fit to month-by-time-control-by-rating-bin cells, with openings aggregated into a retained top-$k$ set plus an “Other” category after sparse cells were excluded. Because classical cells were much less consistently supported after this aggregation and sparse-cell filtering, the retained pooled specification was restricted to blitz and rapid. This restriction preserves the rating-by-time-control comparison in the two best-supported formats while avoiding a comparatively unstable classical contrast. The specification used rating bin, time control, month index, and rating-by-time-control interactions to model opening composition across player-strength strata and formats.

Per-opening negative binomial and weighted least squares models were also fit as lower-complexity alternatives. These models were useful as sensitivity checks because they allowed individual openings to be examined one at a time, but that same feature limited their suitability as the primary model for opening choice. Since they do not model the opening set jointly, they cannot represent substitution across openings in a fully coherent way.

The pooled multinomial model was retained as the primary specification for this subsection. The main reasons were structural appropriateness and competitive held-out performance. It aligned most directly with the compositional form of the outcome while remaining interpretable enough for downstream use in @sec-results. The simpler one-opening alternatives remained useful as supporting checks, but not as the main retained specification.

```{=latex}
\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\caption{Retained pooled multinomial opening-popularity model.}
\label{fig:eq-opening-popularity}

\small
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(Y_i = k)
&=
\frac{\exp(\eta_{i,k})}
{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(\eta_{i,j})},
\quad k=1,\dots,K, \\
\eta_{i,k}
&=
\alpha_k
+
\beta_{1k}\,\mathrm{RatingBin}_i
+
\beta_{2k}\,\mathbf{1}\{c_i=\text{Rapid}\} \\
&\quad
+
\beta_{3k}\,t_i
+
\beta_{4k}\,\mathrm{RatingBin}_i\,\mathbf{1}\{c_i=\text{Rapid}\},
\quad k=1,\dots,K-1, \\
\eta_{i,K}
&=0.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}

\par\medskip
\begin{minipage}{0.92\linewidth}
\footnotesize
Here, $Y_i$ denotes the opening category for month-by-time-control-by-rating-bin cell $i$, $t_i$ is the month index, and $k$ indexes the retained opening categories, including ``Other.'' Blitz is the reference time-control category; classical cells were not included in this pooled specification. Category $K$ is the baseline opening category against which the other opening categories are compared.
\end{minipage}

\end{figure}
```

Robustness checks did not materially alter that decision. Allowing modest nonlinear flexibility in rating changed held-out fit only slightly, while greater flexibility in time did not improve performance enough to justify additional complexity. Varying the number of explicitly modeled openings produced the expected tradeoff between simpler and harder prediction problems, but did not change the broader retention logic. Full model comparisons and supporting diagnostics for this subsection are reported in Appendix [-@sec-appendix-c].


### Time Use {#sec-time-use-2}

Time-use modeling was organized around two related targets— average time use and low-time frequency. Because these outcomes differ in scale and distribution, they were evaluated separately rather than forced into a single retained model family.

For average time use, candidate specifications were compared at both the macro month level and the player-month level. At each level, additive models were compared against interaction specifications that allowed the relationship between rating and time use to vary by time control. The interaction specifications outperformed the corresponding additive alternatives at both analytic levels, even if the numerical improvement was modest. Those gains were directionally consistent and supported the conclusion that a common rating slope across formats was too restrictive for mean time-use modeling. The interaction forms were therefore retained as the primary models for average time use.

```{=latex}
\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\caption{Retained player-level mean time-use model.}
\label{fig:eq-timeuse-mean}

\small
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{AvgTime}_i
&=
\beta_0
+
\beta_1\,\mathrm{Rating}_i
+
\beta_2\,\mathbf{1}\{c_i=\text{Classical}\}
+
\beta_3\,\mathbf{1}\{c_i=\text{Rapid}\} \\
&\quad
+
\beta_4\,\mathrm{Rating}_i\,\mathbf{1}\{c_i=\text{Classical}\}
+
\beta_5\,\mathrm{Rating}_i\,\mathbf{1}\{c_i=\text{Rapid}\}
+
\varepsilon_i.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}

\par\medskip
\begin{minipage}{0.92\linewidth}
\footnotesize
Here, $\mathrm{AvgTime}_i$ denotes average time spent per move for observation $i$. Blitz is the reference time-control category, and the interaction terms allow the rating slope to vary by time control.
\end{minipage}

\end{figure}
```

For low-time frequency, the main comparison was between a fractional quasibinomial specification and a binomial approximation. Since predictive performance did not clearly distinguish the two, model retention was decided on inferential suitability and outcome structure. The fractional quasibinomial was retained because it is better matched to a bounded proportion outcome observed at the cell level, especially when the outcome is concentrated near zero. The binomial approximation remains a useful sensitivity check, but not the primary retained model.

```{=latex}
\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\caption{Retained fractional low-time model.}
\label{fig:eq-timeuse-lowtime}

\small
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{logit}\!\left(\mathbb{E}[L_i \mid X_i]\right)
&=
\beta_0
+
\beta_1\,\mathrm{Rating}_i
+
\beta_2\,\mathbf{1}\{c_i=\text{Classical}\}
+
\beta_3\,\mathbf{1}\{c_i=\text{Rapid}\}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}

\par\medskip
\begin{minipage}{0.92\linewidth}
\footnotesize
Here, $L_i \in [0,1]$ denotes low-time frequency for observation $i$, and $X_i$ contains rating and time-control indicators. Blitz is the reference time-control category.
\end{minipage}

\end{figure}
```

Robustness checks supported both retention decisions. Alternative functional forms produced only limited changes in held-out fit, suggesting that the retained models were not being selected solely because of a narrow specification choice. Detailed comparisons and diagnostics for the time-use models are reported in Appendix [-@sec-appendix-d].


### Player Progression {#sec-player-progression-2}

Player-progression models were designed to assess whether month-$t$ player behavior could be used to predict subsequent rating movement under a forward-in-time design. Three targets were retained for evaluation: 1-month rating change, 3-month rating change, and absolute 1-month rating change. The 3-month target is based on a smaller sample because it requires observing the same player several months later, whereas the 1-month targets preserve substantially more observations. This difference in available support is important context for later comparisons across targets.

The main inferential candidate in this subsection was a player fixed-effects model fit to the player-month panel. This choice followed directly from the substantive goal of the task—  isolating within-player associations between current-month behavior and later rating movement. The baseline feature set included current rating, game volume, average moves, opening diversity, top-opening concentration, and an indicator for whether the player switched their most-played opening. Ridge regression and random forest models were also fit as predictive benchmarks.

Across the retained targets, the player fixed-effects specifications provided the strongest overall combination of longitudinal appropriateness, inferential usefulness, and out-of-sample performance. This made the fixed-effects family the clearest retained direction for the progression task. Among observations for which player fixed effects could be estimated, the panel-based specifications outperformed the predictive benchmarks.

```{=latex}
\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\caption{Generic form of the retained player fixed-effects progression model.}
\label{fig:eq-progression-fe-generic}

\small
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
Y_{i,t}^{(h)}
&=
\alpha_i
+
\beta_1\,\mathrm{AvgRating}_{i,t}
+
\beta_2\,\mathrm{Games}_{i,t}
+
\beta_3\,\mathrm{AvgMoves}_{i,t} \\
&\quad
+
\beta_4\,\mathrm{OpeningDiversity}_{i,t}
+
\beta_5\,\mathrm{TopOpeningShare}_{i,t}
+
\beta_6\,\mathrm{SwitchedOpening}_{i,t}
+
\varepsilon_{i,t}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}

\par\medskip
\begin{minipage}{0.92\linewidth}
\footnotesize
Here, $\alpha_i$ is a player fixed effect, and $Y_{i,t}^{(h)}$ denotes one of three retained progression targets: $\Delta_1\mathrm{Rating}_{i,t}$, $\Delta_3\mathrm{Rating}_{i,t}$, or $|\Delta_1\mathrm{Rating}_{i,t}|$, where $\Delta_h\mathrm{Rating}_{i,t}=\mathrm{Rating}_{i,t+h}-\mathrm{Rating}_{i,t}$.
\end{minipage}

\end{figure}
```

Sensitivity checks further supported that choice. Adding collapsed time-use features on the common-support sample did not improve performance enough to justify the accompanying loss of coverage, and allowing rating to vary nonlinearly produced only a small change relative to the baseline fit. Additional checks also suggested that absorbing common month shocks through added month fixed effects did not improve fit enough to outweigh the cost in simplicity. Full predictive comparisons and supporting robustness checks for this subsection are reported in Appendix [-@sec-appendix-e].


### Player Categorization {#sec-player-categorization-2}

The goal of the player-categorization task was not to identify latent player "types" in a strong inferential sense, but to retain a descriptive specification that could summarize broad behavioral structure in player-month-time-control observations. For that reason, model retention in this subsection emphasized sample coverage, cluster balance, stability, and interpretability rather than formal inferential criteria.

The candidate clustering sample provided complete coverage for repertoire features but only sparse overlap for stable time-use features in the joined design. This made time use unsuitable as a core clustering input in the retained specification. Instead, the retained feature set focused on standardized performance, outcome, repertoire, and activity variables, with time-use measures treated as potential downstream overlays rather than direct inputs to the clustering algorithm.

Candidate descriptive approaches included $k$-means clustering, hierarchical clustering, Gaussian mixture clustering, and dimensionality-reduction methods used in a supporting role. The retained specification used $k$-means with $k = 6$ on the standardized core-plus-repertoire feature set. This solution was preferred because it provided a reasonably balanced partition, used the best-supported merged sample, and remained straightforward to interpret as a descriptive segmentation.

```{=latex}
\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\caption{Retained k-means clustering objective for player categorization.}
\label{fig:eq-categorization-kmeans}

\small
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
\min_{C_1,\dots,C_6}
\sum_{k=1}^{6}
\sum_{i \in C_k}
\left\lVert x_i - \mu_k \right\rVert_2^2.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}

\par\medskip
\begin{minipage}{0.92\linewidth}
\footnotesize
Here, $x_i \in \mathbb{R}^p$ denotes the standardized feature vector for observation $i$, $C_k$ denotes cluster $k$, and $\mu_k$ denotes the centroid of cluster $k$. The retained solution uses six clusters.
\end{minipage}

\end{figure}
```

The robustness and stability checks supported treating the retained clustering solution as useful, but only in a descriptive sense. Relative to the core-only alternative, the core-plus-repertoire feature set yielded a more balanced solution. Repeated $k$-means fits under the retained specification also converged to the same partition, indicating very strong initialization stability. At the same time, agreement with alternative clustering algorithms was only moderate, silhouette values were modest, and month-to-month agreement for overlapping players was limited. These diagnostics suggest that the retained segmentation captures real structure, but not sharply-separated or highly-persistent latent classes. Detailed specification, comparison, and stability diagnostics are reported in Appendix [-@sec-appendix-f].


### Summary {#sec-results-summary}

The retained models define a common analytic strategy across our five empirical domains. Weighted linear and multinomial models were retained for metagame dynamics depending on whether the target was macro or compositional; a pooled multinomial model was retained for opening popularity; interaction-based mean models and a fractional quasibinomial were retained for time use; player fixed-effects models were retained for progression; and a k-means clustering solution based on core-plus-repertoire features was retained for player categorization.

## Results {#sec-results}

This section presents the substantive findings from the retained models described in @sec-modeling. The aim is no longer to compare candidate specifications, but to interpret the model outputs. Accordingly, the section emphasizes interpretable summaries of model output, including estimated effects, representative predicted values, and descriptive profile summaries where appropriate. Additional robustness checks and supplemental diagnostics are reported in Appendices [-@sec-appendix-c], [-@sec-appendix-d], [-@sec-appendix-e], and [-@sec-appendix-f].

### Metagame Dynamics {#sec-metagame-dynamics-3}

The retained metagame models indicate that the opening ecosystem broadened over the study period, although the magnitude of that broadening differed across time controls. The clearest evidence concerns concentration and diversity. Across formats, opening use became less concentrated and the effective number of openings increased, which together indicate gradual metagame diversification rather than convergence onto a narrower set of dominant choices.

Table \ref{tab:metagame-macro-estimates} provides the main inferential summary for the retained macro models. In the baseline format, HHI concentration declined over time while the effective number of openings ($N_{\text{eff}}$) increased, and both trends were larger in rapid and classical than in blitz. These paired results are substantively aligned—  declining concentration and rising effective diversity describe the same underlying shift toward a broader opening ecosystem. The interaction terms matter here because the rate of diversification was not uniform across formats. Relative to blitz, the broadening was more pronounced in rapid and strongest in classical.

@fig-metagame-results makes the same pattern easier to see at the fitted-value level. The concentration curves trend downward over time, while the effective-diversity curves trend upward. The visual impression is not one of sudden disruption or rapid cycling, but of gradual structural widening across the two-year window. This is an important distinction: The metagame appears to be changing through accumulation and redistribution, *not* through abrupt replacement of one dominant opening by another.


```{r Metagame Results Figure}
#| label: fig-metagame-results
#| fig-cap: "Fitted HHI concentration and effective number of openings over time by time control."
#| fig-align: center

p_macro_fit <- readRDS("Paper_files/figure-rds/p_macro_fit.rds")
p_macro_fit
```

By contrast, the retained macro models provide much weaker evidence for systematic time trends in draw rate and average moves. Those outcomes appear comparatively stable over the sample window. Upset rate shows some evidence of a modest positive baseline trend, but that signal is weaker and less consistent across time controls than the concentration and diversity results. This suggests that metagame structure changed more clearly than the broader game environment did.

Overall, the metagame results point to gradual diversification as opposed to convergence. The strongest findings concern ecosystem structure itself, where openings became less concentrated and more diverse, especially in slower formats. The compositional results suggest that this broadening reflects diffuse redistribution across the opening ecosystem rather than a dramatic surge by any single named opening, with some of the increase appearing to occur in the long tail of less-common choices. Changes in draw rate, upset rate, and average moves were much less pronounced, so the main story here is structural broadening in opening choice. Additional metagame comparisons, compositional checks, and supplemental results are reported in Appendix [-@sec-appendix-c].


### Opening Popularity {#sec-opening-popularity-3}

The retained opening-popularity model shows clear differences in opening choice across rating bins and time controls. The most visible pattern is the increasing share of the residual "Other" category as player strength rises.

@fig-opening-popularity-results provides the clearest visual summary of this pattern. In both blitz and rapid, the predicted share of the “Other” category increases with rating.^[Because “Other” aggregates many lower-frequency openings, this pattern should be interpreted as reduced concentration in the retained top set rather than as a single coherent opening category gaining popularity.] This implies that stronger players devote a greater proportion of their games to openings outside the explicitly retained top set. That result does not mean the named openings cease to matter; rather, it means the opening ecosystem becomes less concentrated around the same small group of common labeled choices as rating rises.


```{r Opening-Popularity Results Figure}
#| label: fig-opening-popularity-results
#| fig-cap: "Predicted opening share by rating for selected openings in blitz and rapid."
#| fig-align: center

p_opening_rating <- readRDS("Paper_files/figure-rds/p_opening_rating.rds")
p_opening_rating
```

Table \ref{tab:opening-popularity-rating-profile} provides representative predictions that help anchor the figure. At lower rating levels, more share is allocated to openings such as the Philidor Defense, Scandinavian Defense, and Queen’s Pawn Game. At higher rating levels, the top named openings shift toward alternatives such as the Caro-Kann Defense and the Accelerated London System, while the residual category becomes increasingly dominant. The exact ordering differs somewhat by format, but the broader skill gradient is consistent: Opening popularity is strongly stratified by rating, and time control modifies that structure rather than replacing it.

Temporal changes are present, but modest in magnitude. The over-time movement in the retained multinomial model is directionally consistent with the broader metagame results from @sec-metagame-dynamics-3: The residual “Other” category tends to gain share, while the largest named increases and decreases are comparatively small. This again points away from a story of dramatic named-opening turnover and toward one of distributed compositional change.

The substantive takeaway is that opening choice is highly structured, but most of that structure is cross-sectional as opposed to temporal. Rating and time control organize the opening landscape more strongly than month-to-month drift does. Over time, the opening ecosystem shifts, but the magnitude of that shift is much smaller than the difference between lower- and higher-rated opening distributions. Additional opening-popularity comparisons and supplemental results are reported in Appendix [-@sec-appendix-c].


### Time Use {#sec-time-use-3}

The retained time-use models show that average pacing and low-time pressure capture related but distinct aspects of chess behavior. Across the retained specifications, the most consistent result is that the relationship between rating and average time use differs by time control, while low-time frequency rises with rating in every format.

@fig-time-use-results summarizes these two patterns. For average time spent per move, the rating gradient is negative in blitz but positive in rapid and classical. Higher-rated players therefore move faster on average in blitz, but spend more time per move in slower formats. This means that there is no single monotone relationship between skill and pacing. Instead, the behavioral meaning of a player's use of time depends on the format in which it occurs.


```{r Time-Use Results Figure}
#| label: fig-time-use-results
#| fig-cap: "Predicted average time spent per move and low-time frequency by rating and time control."
#| fig-align: center

p_time_panels <- readRDS("Paper_files/figure-rds/p_time_panels.rds")
p_time_panels
```

The size of the format differences is substantial. Blitz remains the fastest format across the rating range, classical the slowest, and rapid falls between them. More importantly, the slope changes sign across formats, which supports treating time control as more than a nuisance adjustment; it changes the way player strength relates to deliberation time. A single common rating effect would have obscured this distinction.

The low-time results tell a different-yet-complementary story. Low-time frequency increases with rating in blitz, rapid, and classical alike, although the classical estimates are much less precise. The baseline prevalence of low-time states still differs sharply by format – with blitz much higher than rapid or classical – but within each format, stronger players are predicted to enter low-time situations more often. This is important because it shows that low-time frequency is not merely the inverse of average pace. A player can move faster on average and still enter acute time pressure more often, or spend more time on average and also enter low-time states more often.

These results suggest that time management is multi-dimensional; average pace reflects one aspect of behavior, but low-time exposure reflects another. In blitz, stronger players appear to play faster on average while also entering low-time states more often. In rapid and classical, stronger players spend more time on average yet still show higher low-time frequency. This combination implies that stronger players may be allocating time more selectively rather than simply playing uniformly faster or slower. Additional time-use diagnostics, robustness checks, and predicted profiles are reported in Appendix [-@sec-appendix-d].


### Player Progression {#sec-player-progression-3}

The retained player fixed-effects models relate within-player month-to-month behavior to later rating movement. Across the signed-change targets, the clearest positive predictors of later rating gain are average moves, opening diversity, and switching one’s most-played opening. By contrast, game volume and top-opening concentration show weaker and less consistent evidence.

Table \ref{tab:progression-fe-results} provides the central inferential summary. For both the 1-month and 3-month signed targets, higher current average rating is associated with more negative subsequent signed rating change, while average moves, opening diversity, and switching the most-played opening are positively associated with later change. These effects are directionally consistent across the two signed targets, while games played and top-opening share show weaker and less consistent evidence.

@fig-player-progression-results makes the main contrast clearer.^[Coefficients are shown on their original predictor scales and are not directly comparable in magnitude across predictors.] Average moves, opening diversity, and switching one’s most-played opening are positively associated with later signed rating change, while current rating is negatively associated with it. The negative current-rating coefficient likely reflects short-run reversion and the mechanical difficulty of gaining additional rating from a higher current baseline, leaving the more behaviorally interesting signal in game complexity and repertoire adjustment.

```{r Player-Progression Results Figure}
#| label: fig-player-progression-results
#| fig-cap: "Estimated coefficients from the retained player fixed-effects progression models by outcome target."

p_player_coef +
  theme(legend.position = "right")
```

The absolute-change model helps interpret those signed results. None of the favorable signed predictors is positively associated with greater movement magnitude; if anything, average moves, opening diversity, and switching are associated with smaller absolute month-to-month movement. This weakens the interpretation that the signed results are merely artifacts of noisier or more volatile play.

Substantively, the results point toward adaptation and complexity instead of volume alone. Months with longer games, broader repertoires, and a change in the most-played opening are associated with more favorable later signed rating movement, while raw game count is weak and inconclusive once these other behavioral measures are included. These results should still be interpreted as within-player associations, but they consistently suggest that richer and less static opening behavior is more closely linked to later rating gains than sheer activity volume. Additional predictive comparisons, fixed-effects robustness checks, and supplemental results are reported in Appendix [-@sec-appendix-e].


### Player Categorization {#sec-player-categorization-3}

The clusters differ along several behavioral axes at once, including rating, rating differential, game length, repertoire breadth, opening concentration, and opening switching.
