Tables \ref{tab:categorization-performance-profiles} and \ref{tab:categorization-repertoire-profiles} summarize the core descriptive profiles. The clusters are not simply a relabeling of average rating. Instead, they combine performance, repertoire, and game-structure features into distinct configurations. Cluster 1 and Cluster 2 form a particularly clear contrast: Cluster 1 is associated with a broader repertoire, higher rating, and longer games, whereas Cluster 2 is narrower, lower rated, and associated with shorter games. Cluster 3 is especially notable for very high switching, while Cluster 6 is more concentrated and stable in its opening behavior. Clusters 4 and 5 both include relatively stronger players, but Cluster 4 is marked by longer games and lower win rates, while Cluster 5 combines favorable rating differentials with high win rates and narrower repertoires. Collectively, these contrasts suggest that the retained solution is capturing multiple styles of engagement.

The cluster distributions also vary by time control. Some profiles are more common in blitz, while others appear more often in classical, with rapid tending to be more evenly distributed. These differences should not be over-read, especially where classical support is thinner, but they do suggest that format is part of the behavioral structure the clustering solution is capturing. The profiles are therefore not purely abstract player labels; they are partly shaped by the time-control context in which behavior is observed.

```{r Cluster Heatmap}
#| label: fig-cluster-heatmap
#| fig-cap: "Month-to-month transition matrix for the retained player-categorization clusters."
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-pos: H

p_cluster_heatmap <- readRDS("Paper_files/figure-rds/p_transition_heat.rds")
p_cluster_heatmap +
  labs(title = NULL, subtitle = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

@fig-cluster-heatmap helps clarify how these profiles should be interpreted over time. Some clusters show substantial persistence from one month to the next, but switching is also common, and the transition structure is clearly patterned. This is the key reason the clusters are better understood as recurring behavioral states. They capture meaningful structure in player behavior, but that structure appears fluid enough that many players move among states over time instead of remaining locked into a single fixed profile.

This state-based interpretation is consistent with the rest of the paper’s results. The opening ecosystem broadens over time, opening choice varies with strength and format, time use is multi-dimensional, and progression is associated with adaptation. Against that background, recurring-but-fluid behavioral states are a more plausible interpretation than sharply-bounded and permanent classes. Additional clustering specification details, time-control composition summaries, persistence summaries, and robustness diagnostics are reported in Appendix [-@sec-appendix-f].


## Discussion

### Principal Findings {#sec-discussion}

The retained models point to structured variation in online chess behavior across both ecosystem-level and player-level domains. At the ecosystem level, the metagame became less concentrated and more diverse over time. At the opening-choice level, popularity varied systematically by rating and time control. In the time-use domain, average pacing and low-time frequency behaved as related but distinct dimensions of player behavior. In the progression models, favorable later rating movement was associated more consistently with game complexity, repertoire breadth, and repertoire adjustment than with raw activity volume. Finally, the clustering results suggested that player behavior is better summarized as a set of recurring behavioral profiles than as a small number of fixed player types.

In aggregate, these findings argue against simple, one-dimensional explanations. Metagame change was not primarily a story of one opening taking over. Time management was not reducible to a single measure of efficiency. Progression was not best explained by game volume alone. Instead, the results repeatedly point toward diversification, conditional behavior, and adaptation. The subsections that follow interpret those patterns in greater depth and consider what they imply about metagame change, player decision-making, development, and the broader study of online chess behavior.


### Metagame Structure and Opening Choice {#sec-metagame-and-opening-discussion}

The strongest ecosystem-level finding was the paired decline in concentration and rise in effective diversity across time controls. In substantive terms, the metagame broadened over the study period. That result matters because a common expectation in competitive environments is some degree of convergence toward a relatively narrow set of dominant strategies, especially when players have broad access to shared theory, engine analysis, and educational content. The present results instead suggest a more expansive pattern, in which opening use became less concentrated rather than more so.

That conclusion should still be interpreted cautiously. Our results do not identify the mechanism behind this broadening, nor can they determine whether the same pattern would appear on other platforms or in other eras of online chess. Even so, the outcome is notable. One plausible interpretation is that large online player populations support a wider range of viable strategic habits than a narrower or more homogeneous competitive environment would. Another is simply that chess is strategically rich enough that increased access to information does not mechanically force population behavior into a small set of dominant lines.

The opening-popularity results sharpen that picture. Opening choice varied much more clearly by rating and time control than by calendar time. Stronger players allocated less share to the most common named openings and more to the residual “Other” category, while time control modified that structure rather than replacing it. Temporal movement was directionally consistent with the broader metagame results, but comparatively modest in magnitude. The opening landscape therefore looks less like a rapidly-rotating cycle of named openings and more like a layered system of skill-stratified preferences with gradual long-run drift.

It is also useful to distinguish between two kinds of diversification. One possibility would be simple turnover among the same small set of highly popular openings. The other, which is more consistent with the present results, is a broader expansion in the share allocated outside that narrow top set. The latter interpretation is more substantively important, because it suggests widening participation in the opening space rather than mere reshuffling among a fixed group of choices.

Overall, these results support a picture of gradual diversification rather than convergence, with broadening driven more by long-tail expansion and skill-stratified choice than by visible turnover among a small set of named openings.


### Time Management as Multi-Dimensional Behavior {#sec-time-discussion}

The time-use results suggest that time management is not a one-dimensional behavioral trait. Average time use and low-time frequency are related, but they capture different aspects of play. Across formats, the relationship between rating and average time use changed sign: Stronger players moved faster on average in blitz, but used more time on average in rapid and classical. At the same time, low-time frequency increased with rating in every format.

This matters because it changes the way time use should be interpreted. In blitz, faster average play among stronger players may reflect greater fluency, pattern recognition, or reliance on stable priors. In slower formats, greater average time use may instead reflect deeper calculation, more deliberate planning, or a higher willingness to invest time in critical positions. The same amount of time spent per move therefore does not have the same meaning across formats. Time control is not merely a nuisance adjustment; it changes the behavioral interpretation of pacing itself.

The low-time results reinforce that point. A simple expectation might be that stronger players use time more smoothly and therefore avoid acute time pressure. The retained models suggest otherwise. Stronger players were more likely to enter low-time states in blitz, rapid, and classical alike. This does not imply poor time management. Rather, it suggests that stronger players may allocate time more selectively, accepting later pressure in exchange for deeper thinking when they judge it worthwhile.

Together, these findings support a view of time management as multi-dimensional. Baseline pace and acute time-pressure exposure are not interchangeable, and neither can be reduced to a single global measure of “better” or “worse” time use. More broadly, the results suggest that time management is itself a meaningful behavioral domain rather than merely a mechanical byproduct of format.


### Progression, Adaptation, and Player Development {#sec-player-progression-discussion}

A simple expectation about skill development is that more practice should lead to more improvement. In the context of online chess, that expectation would imply that raw activity volume is the strongest predictor of subsequent rating gains. The retained progression models did not support that view. Instead, more favorable later rating movement was associated more consistently with longer games, greater opening diversity, and switching the most-played opening. By contrast, games played was comparatively weak and inconclusive once these other behavioral measures were included.

This pattern suggests that player development may depend more on the character of engagement than on volume alone. Broader repertoires and changes in the most-played opening are consistent with adaptation, experimentation, or strategic flexibility. Longer games may likewise reflect more complex or demanding play. None of these interpretations can be treated as causal, but together they support a developmental account in which richer engagement matters more than repetition by itself.

The absolute-change model further clarifies the signed-change results. The predictors associated with favorable signed rating movement were not associated with larger absolute swings. If anything, average moves, opening diversity, and switching were associated with smaller absolute month-to-month movement. That pattern weakens the interpretation that the signed results are merely artifacts of noisier or more volatile play. The progression findings therefore do not look like a story of high-risk experimentation producing bigger swings in either direction. They look more like a story of gradual improvement associated with adaptation and complexity.

This does not mean that playing more games is irrelevant. A more careful interpretation is that raw volume has limited additional explanatory value once more behaviorally informative measures are taken into account. In that sense, the retained models suggest diminishing returns to volume alone and a stronger role for adaptive engagement. Improvement, at least in this setting, appears better characterized as an adaptive process than as a purely cumulative one.


### Behavioral Profiles as Descriptive States {#sec-categorization-discussion}

The clustering results are best interpreted descriptively. They do not justify strong inferential claims about latent player “types,” but they do indicate that player-month observations contain enough structure to be grouped into recurring behavioral profiles. Those profiles vary along multiple axes at once, including skill, repertoire breadth, opening concentration, switching behavior, game length, and outcome structure. That is important because it means the clustering solution is not merely reproducing the platform’s rating hierarchy under a different name.

The retained profiles are most naturally interpreted as states rather than fixed identities. Some persistence is clearly present, but so are patterned transitions between clusters. Players do not appear to remain locked into a single behavioral class over time. Instead, the evidence suggests movement among recurring configurations of behavior. That reading is consistent with the rest of the paper’s findings: The opening environment broadens over time, time use depends on context, and progression is associated with adaptation rather than rigidity. Against that background, recurring-but-fluid behavioral states are a more plausible interpretation than sharply-bounded and permanent player types.

This interpretation also helps explain why the clustering results are useful despite their inferential limits. Their value does not come from proving the existence of a small number of true latent player categories. It comes from showing that player behavior is structured enough to support interpretable recurring profiles. That in turn suggests a promising direction for later work— modeling movement among behavioral states directly.


### Practical Uses and Broader Implications {#sec-implications-discussion}

Methodologically, the project shows that linked models of metagame structure, opening choice, time use, progression, and behavioral profiling can be integrated within a single analytic framework. These domains are often studied separately, but the present results suggest that they are better understood as linked parts of a broader behavioral system.

The results also point to possible practical uses in coaching or player-development settings. The progression models suggest that broader and more adaptive engagement may be more informative than game volume alone. The time-use results suggest that average pace and low-time pressure should be treated as distinct aspects of behavior rather than collapsed into one summary metric. Together, these findings suggest that player-facing tools may be more useful when they track repertoire breadth, adjustment, and time-use patterns alongside more familiar performance measures.

More broadly, the paper shows that large-scale online game logs can support behavioral analysis without reducing chess to engine evaluation alone. Chess is especially well suited to this kind of work because it combines standardized rules, rich decision structure, repeated play, and a mature rating system. As a result, it offers a useful environment for studying adaptation, strategic diversity, and development in a naturally occurring competitive setting.


### Limitations {#sec-limitations-discussion}

The most important limitation of the project is that it is observational throughout. The results support associations, not causal claims. For example, opening diversity and repertoire adjustment are associated with more favorable later rating movement, but the models do not establish that increasing diversity or switching openings causes improvement. Likewise, the time-use results describe behavioral signatures associated with skill and format, not causal mechanisms of stronger play. Even the fixed-effects models, while stronger than purely cross-sectional comparisons, do not eliminate time-varying confounding.

A second limitation concerns data scope and analytic breadth. The project was intentionally designed to be reproducible and to address several substantive questions within one framework. That choice made the analysis broader, but it also constrained how deeply any one domain could be modeled. A more specialized study could devote more of the sample, feature design, and model structure to a single problem, such as move-level decision quality, richer opening taxonomy, or transition dynamics among behavioral profiles.

The models also compress a strategically complex environment into tractable summaries. That compression is unavoidable. Chess is too rich to model exhaustively at scale, so each analytic task relies on reduced representations of a much more detailed behavioral space. Some simplifications are especially visible in the opening models, which rely on a top-$k$ structure with a substantively meaningful but still heterogeneous “Other” category, and in the use of relatively simple functional forms in several retained models. These choices are reasonable for the present project, but they still limit how finely the results can characterize behavior.

Finally, the findings are specific to the Lichess platform and to the January 2024 through December 2025 study window. They should therefore be interpreted as results about that setting, not as definitive descriptions of online chess as a whole. Other platforms, populations, or periods may display similar patterns, but they may also differ in meaningful ways.


### Future Work {#sec-future-work}

A natural next step is to apply the retained framework more deeply within specific domains. Especially promising directions include move-level decision-quality analysis, richer opening annotation, longer player histories, and explicit modeling of transitions among behavioral profiles. These extensions would preserve the present paper’s core structure while allowing much deeper treatment of individual behavioral domains.

Several specific empirical questions also follow directly from the present results. One is whether metagame broadening reflects genuine experimentation or primarily long-tail expansion in opening choice. Another is whether the higher low-time frequency observed among stronger players reflects sharper positions, more selective time investment, or some other feature of high-level play. A third is whether repertoire adjustment is a precursor to improvement or merely one correlate of broader behavioral change. These questions are not fully answerable within the current design, but they are clearly motivated by the retained findings.

A final priority is external validation. Because the results are tied to one platform and one time window, cross-platform and cross-period replication would be especially valuable. Replication on other platforms, or on earlier and later Lichess periods, would help distinguish patterns that are specific to this environment from those that are more general features of online chess. If the framework proves stable across settings, it could support a broader comparative research program on strategic behavior and skill development in competitive online environments.

## Data Reference and Construction {#sec-appendix-a}

### Variable Definitions

```{=latex}
\begin{xltabular}[l]{\textwidth}{@{}l l X@{}}
\caption{Variable definitions for the player-month (\texttt{pm}) table.}
\label{tab:variables-pm}\\

\toprule
\textbf{Variable} & \textbf{Type} & \textbf{Description} \\
\midrule
\endfirsthead

\toprule
\textbf{Variable} & \textbf{Type} & \textbf{Description} \\
\midrule
\endhead

\midrule
\multicolumn{3}{r}{\small\emph{Continued...}} \\
\endfoot

\bottomrule
\endlastfoot

\texttt{player} & categorical & Deterministic pseudonymous user ID (e.g., \texttt{u\us 01234567abcdefgh}). Identifies a player across months in longitudinal summaries. \\
\texttt{month} & categorical & Month of play as \texttt{YYYY-MM}. Primary time index for longitudinal analysis. \\
\texttt{games} & numeric (count) & Number of games played by the player in the month. Also a reliability/weighting signal. \\
\texttt{wins} & numeric (count) & Count of wins in the month. \\
\texttt{losses} & numeric (count) & Count of losses in the month. \\
\texttt{draws} & numeric (count) & Count of draws in the month. \\
\texttt{win\us rate} & numeric (proportion) & Wins divided by games. Primary performance measure in player-level models. \\
\texttt{draw\us rate} & numeric (proportion) & Draws divided by games. Useful because draw propensity varies by skill and style. \\
\texttt{avg\us rating} & numeric & Average of the player’s pre-game rating across games in the month. Primary skill proxy. \\
\texttt{avg\us opp\us rating} & numeric & Average opponent pre-game rating in the month. Contextualizes performance and approximates strength of schedule. \\
\texttt{avg\us rating\us diff} & numeric & Average (player rating minus opponent rating) across games in the month. Summarizes typical matchup difficulty. \\
\texttt{avg\us moves} & numeric & Average game length in moves. Proxy for style and game complexity. \\
\texttt{opening\us diversity} & numeric (count) & Number of distinct openings used in the month. Proxy for repertoire breadth. \\
\texttt{top\us opening} & categorical & Most frequently played opening during the month (ties broken deterministically). Summary of dominant repertoire choice. \\
\end{xltabular}
```

```{=latex}
\begin{xltabular}[l]{\textwidth}{@{}l l X@{}}
\caption{Variable definitions for the player-month-by-time-control (\texttt{pm\us tc}) table.}
\label{tab:variables-pm-tc}\\

\toprule
\textbf{Variable} & \textbf{Type} & \textbf{Description} \\
\midrule
\endfirsthead

\toprule
\textbf{Variable} & \textbf{Type} & \textbf{Description} \\
\midrule
\endhead

\midrule
\multicolumn{3}{r}{\small\emph{Continued...}} \\
\endfoot

\bottomrule
\endlastfoot

\texttt{player} & categorical & Deterministic pseudonymous user ID. Identifies a player across months and time controls. \\
\texttt{month} & categorical & Month of play as \texttt{YYYY-MM}. Primary time index for player-period analysis. \\
\texttt{tc\us bucket} & categorical & Time control bucket: \texttt{blitz}, \texttt{rapid}, or \texttt{classical}. Stratifies behavior by constraint level. \\
\texttt{games} & numeric (count) & Number of games played by the player in the month/time-control cell. Reliability/weighting signal. \\
\texttt{wins} & numeric (count) & Count of wins in the cell. \\
\texttt{losses} & numeric (count) & Count of losses in the cell. \\
\texttt{draws} & numeric (count) & Count of draws in the cell. \\
\texttt{win\us rate} & numeric (proportion) & Wins divided by games in the month/time-control cell. \\
\texttt{draw\us rate} & numeric (proportion) & Draws divided by games in the cell. Useful because draw prevalence varies by time control. \\
\texttt{avg\us rating} & numeric & Average of the player’s pre-game rating across games in the cell. Primary skill proxy within time control. \\
\texttt{avg\us opp\us rating} & numeric & Average opponent pre-game rating in the cell. Contextualizes performance within format. \\
\texttt{avg\us rating\us diff} & numeric & Average (player rating minus opponent rating) in the cell. Summarizes typical matchup difficulty. \\
\texttt{avg\us moves} & numeric & Average game length in moves for the cell. Proxy for style/complexity within format. \\
\texttt{opening\us diversity} & numeric (count) & Number of distinct openings used in the cell. Proxy for repertoire breadth within format. \\
\texttt{top\us opening} & categorical & Most frequently played opening in the cell (ties broken deterministically). \\
\end{xltabular}
```

```{=latex}
\begin{xltabular}[l]{\textwidth}{@{}l l X@{}}
\caption{Variable definitions for the player-opening summary (\texttt{pom\us tc}) table.}
\label{tab:variables-pom-tc}\\

\toprule
\textbf{Variable} & \textbf{Type} & \textbf{Description} \\
\midrule
\endfirsthead

\toprule
\textbf{Variable} & \textbf{Type} & \textbf{Description} \\
\midrule
\endhead

\midrule
\multicolumn{3}{r}{\small\emph{Continued...}} \\
\endfoot

\bottomrule
\endlastfoot

\texttt{player} & categorical & Deterministic pseudonymous user ID. Identifies the player whose repertoire entry is being summarized. \\
\texttt{month} & categorical & Month of play as \texttt{YYYY-MM}. Time index for repertoire analysis. \\
\texttt{tc\us bucket} & categorical & Time control bucket: \texttt{blitz}, \texttt{rapid}, or \texttt{classical}. \\
\texttt{eco} & categorical & ECO opening code (e.g., \texttt{C41}). Standardized opening taxonomy. \\
\texttt{opening} & categorical & Human-readable opening family name. Main opening identifier for repertoire analysis. \\
\texttt{games} & numeric (count) & Number of games the player used the opening in the month/time-control cell. Frequency weight. \\
\texttt{win\us rate} & numeric (proportion) & Opening-specific win rate for the player in the cell. Used to study effectiveness conditional on opening. \\
\texttt{draw\us rate} & numeric (proportion) & Opening-specific draw rate for the player in the cell. Helps characterize risk profile and style. \\
\texttt{avg\us rating} & numeric & Average player rating in games where the opening was played. Enables comparison of opening choice across skill. \\
\texttt{avg\us rating\us diff} & numeric & Average rating difference in games where the opening was played. Captures whether openings are used in tougher or easier matchups. \\
\end{xltabular}
```

```{=latex}
\begin{xltabular}[l]{\textwidth}{@{}l l X@{}}
\caption{Variable definitions for the player time-use summary (\texttt{ptm\us tc}) table.}
\label{tab:variables-ptm-tc}\\

\toprule
\textbf{Variable} & \textbf{Type} & \textbf{Description} \\
\midrule
\endfirsthead

\toprule
\textbf{Variable} & \textbf{Type} & \textbf{Description} \\
\midrule
\endhead

\midrule
\multicolumn{3}{r}{\small\emph{Continued...}} \\
\endfoot

\bottomrule
\endlastfoot

\texttt{player} & categorical & Deterministic pseudonymous user ID. Identifies the player in the time-use summary. \\
\texttt{month} & categorical & Month of play as \texttt{YYYY-MM}. Time index for player-period time-use analysis. \\
\texttt{tc\us bucket} & categorical & Time control bucket: \texttt{blitz}, \texttt{rapid}, or \texttt{classical}. \\
\texttt{move\us rows} & numeric (count) & Number of sampled move observations contributing to the summary. Primary reliability signal. \\
\texttt{games} & numeric (count) & Number of distinct games contributing move records to the player-month-time-control cell. \\
\texttt{avg\us time\us spent} & numeric (seconds) & Mean time spent per move. Captures typical deliberation time. \\
\texttt{median\us time\us spent} & numeric (seconds) & Median time spent per move; robust to outliers and occasional long thinks. \\
\texttt{p90\us time\us spent} & numeric (seconds) & 90th percentile of time spent per move. Measures the upper tail of thinking time and occasional deep calculation. \\
\texttt{avg\us clock\us after} & numeric (seconds) & Mean remaining clock time after moves. Proxy for time management and pacing. \\
\texttt{low\us time\us rate} & numeric (proportion) & Fraction of sampled moves flagged as low-time. Proxy for time-trouble frequency. \\
\texttt{avg\us rating} & numeric & Average player rating across sampled move records in the cell. Allows stratification by skill. \\
\texttt{avg\us rating\us diff} & numeric & Average rating difference across sampled move records in the cell. Controls for opponent-strength effects. \\
\texttt{avg\us time\us opening} & numeric (seconds) & Average time spent per move in the opening interval, defined as moves 1–10. \\
\texttt{avg\us time\us middlegame} & numeric (seconds) & Average time spent per move in the middlegame interval, defined as moves 11–25. May be missing for cells with no sampled moves in this range. \\
\texttt{avg\us time\us endgame} & numeric (seconds) & Average time spent per move in the endgame interval, defined as moves 26 and later. Often missing because many games do not reach this threshold. \\
\end{xltabular}
```

```{=latex}
\begin{xltabular}[l]{\textwidth}{@{}l l X@{}}

\label{tab:variables-mom-tc}\\

\toprule
\textbf{Variable} & \textbf{Type} & \textbf{Description} \\
\midrule
\endfirsthead

\toprule
\textbf{Variable} & \textbf{Type} & \textbf{Description} \\
\midrule
\endhead

\midrule
\multicolumn{3}{r}{\small\emph{Continued...}} \\
\endfoot

\bottomrule
\endlastfoot

\texttt{month} & categorical & Month of play as \texttt{YYYY-MM}. Primary time index for metagame analysis. \\
\texttt{tc\us bucket} & categorical & Time control bucket: \texttt{blitz}, \texttt{rapid}, or \texttt{classical}. \\
\texttt{eco} & categorical & ECO opening code. Standardized opening taxonomy useful for grouping openings into families. \\
\texttt{opening} & categorical & Human-readable opening family name. Primary opening identifier in population-level summaries. \\
\texttt{games} & numeric (count) & Number of sampled games for the opening within the month/time-control cell. Precision/support indicator. \\
\texttt{share} & numeric (proportion) & Fraction of sampled games in the month/time-control cell using the opening. Core metagame-adoption measure. \\
\texttt{white\us win\us rate} & numeric (proportion) & Fraction of games in the cell that White wins. Used for opening-level success patterns and color asymmetries. \\
\texttt{black\us win\us rate} & numeric (proportion) & Fraction of games in the cell that Black wins. Complements \texttt{white\us win\us rate}. \\
\texttt{draw\us rate} & numeric (proportion) & Fraction of games in the cell that end in a draw. Draw propensity varies by opening and time control. \\
\texttt{upset\us rate} & numeric (proportion) & Fraction of games in which the lower-rated player wins (pipeline definition). Proxy for volatility and competitiveness. \\
\texttt{avg\us abs\us rating\us diff} & numeric & Mean absolute rating gap between players in the opening/month/time-control cell. Context for outcome rates. \\
\texttt{avg\us moves} & numeric & Mean game length in moves for the opening/month/time-control cell. Proxy for complexity and style at the population level. \\
\end{xltabular}
```

```{=latex}
\begin{xltabular}[l]{\textwidth}{@{}l l X@{}}
\caption{Variable definitions for the metagame month-level summary (\texttt{mm\us tc}) table.}
\label{tab:variables-mm-tc}\\

\toprule
\textbf{Variable} & \textbf{Type} & \textbf{Description} \\
\midrule
\endfirsthead

\toprule
\textbf{Variable} & \textbf{Type} & \textbf{Description} \\
\midrule
\endhead

\midrule
\multicolumn{3}{r}{\small\emph{Continued...}} \\
\endfoot

\bottomrule
\endlastfoot

\texttt{month} & categorical & Month of play as \texttt{YYYY-MM}. Time index for broad metagame summaries. \\
\texttt{tc\us bucket} & categorical & Time control bucket: \texttt{blitz}, \texttt{rapid}, or \texttt{classical}. \\
\texttt{games} & numeric (count) & Number of sampled games in the month/time-control cell. Precision/support indicator and denominator for aggregate rates. \\
\texttt{avg\us white\us rating} & numeric & Mean pre-game rating of White across sampled games in the cell. Summarizes the average strength of White players in that slice of the metagame. \\
\texttt{avg\us black\us rating} & numeric & Mean pre-game rating of Black across sampled games in the cell. Complements \texttt{avg\us white\us rating}. \\
\texttt{avg\us abs\us rating\us diff} & numeric & Mean absolute rating gap between players in the cell. Context for outcome rates and competitiveness. \\
\texttt{avg\us moves} & numeric & Mean game length in moves for the cell. Proxy for overall complexity and style at the month/time-control level. \\
\texttt{white\us win\us rate} & numeric (proportion) & Fraction of games in the cell that White wins. Useful for broad color-balance and outcome summaries by format and month. \\
\texttt{black\us win\us rate} & numeric (proportion) & Fraction of games in the cell that Black wins. Complements \texttt{white\us win\us rate}. \\
\texttt{draw\us rate} & numeric (proportion) & Fraction of games in the cell that end in a draw. Draw prevalence varies by time control and month. \\
\texttt{upset\us rate} & numeric (proportion) & Fraction of games in which the lower-rated player wins (pipeline definition). Proxy for volatility and competitive unpredictability. \\
\texttt{opening\us distinct} & numeric (count) & Number of distinct openings observed in the month/time-control cell. Summary measure of metagame breadth or opening variety. \\
\end{xltabular}
```

```{=latex}
\begin{xltabular}[l]{\textwidth}{@{}l l X@{}}

\multicolumn{3}{r}{\small\emph{Continued...}} \\
\endfoot

\endlastfoot

\texttt{month} & categorical & Month of play as \texttt{YYYY-MM}. Time index for population-level time-use summaries. \\
\texttt{tc\us bucket} & categorical & Time control bucket: \texttt{blitz}, \texttt{rapid}, or \texttt{classical}. \\
\texttt{move\us rows} & numeric (count) & Number of sampled move observations contributing to the month/time-control summary. Primary support indicator. \\
\texttt{games} & numeric (count) & Number of distinct games contributing move records to the cell. Useful for distinguishing move-level and game-level support. \\
\texttt{avg\us time\us spent} & numeric (seconds) & Mean time spent per move across all sampled moves in the cell. Captures overall deliberation time at the population level. \\
\texttt{median\us time\us spent} & numeric (seconds) & Median time spent per move in the cell. Robust to outliers and long individual thinks. \\
\texttt{p90\us time\us spent} & numeric (seconds) & 90th percentile of time spent per move in the cell. Measures the upper tail of thinking time. \\
\texttt{avg\us clock\us after} & numeric (seconds) & Mean remaining clock time after moves in the cell. Proxy for overall pacing and time-management style by month and format. \\
\texttt{low\us time\us rate} & numeric (proportion) & Fraction of sampled moves in the cell flagged as low-time. Population-level measure of time-trouble frequency. \\
\end{xltabular}
```

## Exploratory Diagnostics and Support {#sec-appendix-b}

### Reliability

```{r Reliability Plot}
#| label: fig-reliability
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of games per player-month in the sampled panel."
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-pos: H
#| fig-height: 3

gdist <- dbGetQuery(con, sprintf("
  SELECT games
  FROM read_parquet(%s)
  WHERE games <= 250
", qpath(paths$pm)))

ggplot(gdist, aes(x=games)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "steelblue", color = "steelblue") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 250)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  labs(x = "Games per Player in a Given Month", y = "Rows") +
  theme_few()
```

```{r Coverage-by-Rating Plot}
#| label: fig-coverage-rating
#| fig-cap: "Support across rating bins by time control, shown as row counts and summed games in `pom_tc`."
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-pos: H
#| fig-height: 3

bin_width <- 200

support_by_rating2 <- dbGetQuery(con, sprintf("
  SELECT
    tc_bucket,
    CAST(FLOOR(avg_rating / %d) * %d AS INTEGER) AS rating_bin,
    COUNT(*) AS n_rows,
    SUM(games) AS total_games
  FROM read_parquet(%s)
  WHERE avg_rating IS NOT NULL
    AND games IS NOT NULL
    AND tc_bucket IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY tc_bucket, rating_bin
  ORDER BY tc_bucket, rating_bin
", bin_width, bin_width, qpath(paths$pm_tc))) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(n_rows, total_games),
    names_to = "measure",
    values_to = "support"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    measure = recode(
      measure,
      n_rows = "Row Count",
      total_games = "Summed Games"
    ),
    tc_bucket = factor(tc_bucket, levels = c("blitz", "rapid", "classical"))
  )

ggplot(support_by_rating2, aes(x = rating_bin, y = support, fill = tc_bucket, group = tc_bucket)) +
  geom_col(width = bin_width * 0.9) +
  facet_grid(
    measure ~ tc_bucket,
    scales = "free_y",
    labeller = labeller(
      tc_bucket = c(blitz = "Blitz", rapid = "Rapid", classical = "Classical")
    )
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = pretty_breaks(n = 7)) +
  labs(
    x = "Rating Bin",
    y = NULL,
  ) +
  scale_fill_few() +
  theme_few() +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(linewidth = 0.3, colour = "grey85"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "none"
  )
```

```{r Rating Changes Plot}
#| label: fig-delta-rating

chg <- dbGetQuery(con, sprintf("
  WITH x AS (
    SELECT player, month, avg_rating
    FROM read_parquet(%s)
  ),
  y AS (
    SELECT
      player,
      month,
      avg_rating,
      LAG(avg_rating) OVER (PARTITION BY player ORDER BY month) AS prev_rating
    FROM x
  )
  SELECT (avg_rating - prev_rating) AS d_rating
  FROM y
  WHERE prev_rating IS NOT NULL AND d_rating >= -300 AND d_rating <= 300
", qpath(paths$pm)))

ggplot(chg, aes(x=d_rating)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=80, fill = "steelblue", color = "steelblue") +
  labs(x = "Month-to-Month Change in Average Rating", y = "Count") +
  theme_few()
```

### Time-Pressure Diagnostics

```{r LTD}
#| label: fig-low-time-distribution
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of low-time rate and exact-zero mass by time control."
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-pos: H


min_moves_ptm <- 30
positive_binwidth <- 0.01

tc_levels <- c("blitz", "rapid", "classical")
tc_labels <- c(
  blitz = "Blitz",
  rapid = "Rapid",
  classical = "Classical"
)

ltr_dist <- dbGetQuery(con, sprintf("
  SELECT
    tc_bucket,
    low_time_rate,
    move_rows
  FROM read_parquet(%s)
  WHERE tc_bucket IS NOT NULL
    AND low_time_rate IS NOT NULL
    AND move_rows IS NOT NULL
    AND move_rows >= %d
", qpath(paths$ptm_tc), min_moves_ptm)) |>
  mutate(tc_bucket = factor(tc_bucket, levels = tc_levels))

zero_panel <- ltr_dist |>
  mutate(
    panel = "Zero mass",
    x_cat = if_else(low_time_rate == 0, "0%", ">0%")
  ) |>
  count(tc_bucket, panel, x_cat, name = "n")

positive_panel <- ltr_dist |>
  filter(low_time_rate > 0) |>
  mutate(panel = "Positive support")

p1 <- ggplot(zero_panel, aes(x = x_cat, y = n, fill = tc_bucket, group = tc_bucket)) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(
    ~tc_bucket,
    labeller = as_labeller(tc_labels)
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  labs(
    x = "Exact-Zero Mass",
    y = "Rows"
  ) +
  scale_fill_few(drop = FALSE) +
  theme_few() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

p2 <- ggplot(positive_panel, aes(x = low_time_rate, fill = tc_bucket, group = tc_bucket)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = positive_binwidth, boundary = 0) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~tc_bucket,
    scales = "free_y",
    labeller = as_labeller(tc_labels)
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  labs(
    x = "Low-Time Rate",
    y = "Rows"
  ) +
  scale_fill_few(drop = FALSE) +
  theme_few() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

p2 / p1
```

```{r LTR}
#| label: fig-low-time
#| fig-cap: "Next-month rating change by low-time rate, pooled across time controls."
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-pos: H

min_games_pm <- 5 # require at least this many games in the month (across all TCs)
min_moves_ptm <- 25 # require at least this many move rows in the month (across all TCs)

ltr_scatter_all <- dbGetQuery(con, sprintf("
  WITH pm_tc AS (
    SELECT
      player,
      month,
      avg_rating,
      games
    FROM read_parquet(%s)
    WHERE player IS NOT NULL
      AND month  IS NOT NULL
      AND avg_rating IS NOT NULL
      AND games IS NOT NULL
  ),
  pm AS (
    -- collapse across time controls using games-weighted avg_rating
    SELECT
      player,
      month,
      SUM(games) AS games_total,
      SUM(avg_rating * games) / SUM(games) AS avg_rating_all
    FROM pm_tc
    GROUP BY player, month
    HAVING SUM(games) >= %d
  ),
  pm_next AS (
    SELECT
      player,
      month,
      games_total,
      avg_rating_all,
      LEAD(avg_rating_all) OVER (PARTITION BY player ORDER BY month) AS next_rating_all
    FROM pm
  ),
  delta AS (
    SELECT
      player,
      month,
      games_total,
      avg_rating_all,
      (next_rating_all - avg_rating_all) AS d_rating_next
    FROM pm_next
    WHERE next_rating_all IS NOT NULL
  ),
  ptm_tc AS (
    SELECT
      player,
      month,
      low_time_rate,
      move_rows
    FROM read_parquet(%s)
    WHERE player IS NOT NULL
      AND month  IS NOT NULL
      AND low_time_rate IS NOT NULL
      AND move_rows IS NOT NULL
  ),
  ptm AS (
    -- collapse across time controls using move_rows-weighted low_time_rate
    SELECT
      player,
      month,
      SUM(move_rows) AS move_rows_total,
      SUM(low_time_rate * move_rows) / SUM(move_rows) AS low_time_rate_all
    FROM ptm_tc
    GROUP BY player, month
    HAVING SUM(move_rows) >= %d
  )
  SELECT
    d.player,
    d.month,
    d.avg_rating_all,
    d.games_total,
    d.d_rating_next,
    p.low_time_rate_all,
    p.move_rows_total
  FROM delta d
  JOIN ptm p USING (player, month)
", qpath(paths$pm_tc), min_games_pm,
   qpath(paths$ptm_tc), min_moves_ptm))

ggplot(ltr_scatter_all, aes(x = low_time_rate_all, y = d_rating_next)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.25) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  ylim(-225, 225) +
  labs(
    x = "Low-Time Rate",
    y = "Next-Month Rating Change"
  ) +
  theme_few()
```

### Supplemental Exploratory Plots by Topic

```{r Opening Trends Helper}
plot_opening_trends <- function(tc_use, fig_title) {
  top_openings <- dbGetQuery(con, sprintf("
    WITH x AS (
      SELECT opening, SUM(games) AS total_games
      FROM read_parquet(%s)
      WHERE tc_bucket='%s' AND opening IS NOT NULL
      GROUP BY opening
    )
    SELECT opening
    FROM x
    ORDER BY total_games DESC
    LIMIT 8
  ", qpath(paths$mom_tc), tc_use))

  open_list <- paste0("('", paste(gsub("'", "''", top_openings$opening), collapse="','"), "')")

  trend <- dbGetQuery(con, sprintf("
    WITH filtered AS (
      SELECT month, tc_bucket, opening, games
      FROM read_parquet(%s)
      WHERE tc_bucket='%s'
        AND opening IN %s
        AND opening IS NOT NULL
    ),
    opening_level AS (
      SELECT
        month,
        tc_bucket,
        opening,
        SUM(games) AS games
      FROM filtered
      GROUP BY month, tc_bucket, opening
    )
    SELECT
      month,
      tc_bucket,
      opening,
      games,
      CAST(games AS DOUBLE) / SUM(games) OVER (PARTITION BY month, tc_bucket) AS share
    FROM opening_level
    ORDER BY month, opening
  ", qpath(paths$mom_tc), tc_use, open_list)) |>
    mutate(
      month_date = as.Date(paste0(month, "-01"))
    )

  ggplot(trend, aes(x = month_date, y = share, color = opening, group = opening)) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
    scale_x_date(
      limits = as.Date(c("2024-01-01", "2025-12-01")),
      breaks = as.Date(c("2024-03-01", "2024-06-01", "2024-09-01", "2024-12-01", "2025-03-01", "2025-06-01", "2025-09-01", "2025-12-01")),
      date_labels = "%Y-%m"
    ) +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 0.1)) +
    labs(
      x = "Month",
      y = "Share of Games",
      color = ""
    ) +
    scale_color_few(labels = function(x) str_wrap(x, width = 28)) +
    theme_few() +
    theme(
      panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major.y = element_line(linewidth = 0.3, colour = "grey85"),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      legend.position = "bottom",
      axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
    ) +
    guides(color = guide_legend(nrow = 4, byrow = TRUE))
}
```

```{r Allocation Profile by Rating}
#| label: fig-time-allocation

phase <- dbGetQuery(con, sprintf("
  SELECT
    tc_bucket,
    FLOOR(avg_rating/200)*200 AS rating_bin,
    AVG(avg_time_opening) AS t_open,
    AVG(avg_time_middlegame) AS t_mid,
    AVG(avg_time_endgame) AS t_end,
    SUM(move_rows) AS total_moves
  FROM read_parquet(%s)
  GROUP BY tc_bucket, rating_bin
  HAVING total_moves >= 10000
  ORDER BY tc_bucket, rating_bin
", qpath(paths$ptm_tc)))

phase_long <- phase |>
  pivot_longer(cols=c(t_open, t_mid, t_end),
                      names_to="phase", values_to="sec")

ggplot(phase_long, aes(x=rating_bin, y=sec, color=phase, group=phase)) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~factor(tc_bucket, levels = c("blitz", "rapid", "classical")), scales="free_y", labeller = as_labeller(c(
      blitz = "Blitz",
      rapid = "Rapid",
      classical = "Classical"
    ))) +
  labs(x="Rating", y="Average Time per Move (Seconds)", color = "Phase") +
  scale_color_fivethirtyeight(labels = c("Endgame", "Middlegame", "Opening")) +
  theme_few() + 
  theme(
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(linewidth = 0.3, colour = "grey85"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )
```

```{r Div Strata}
#| label: fig-strata
#| fig-cap: "Mean next-month rating change by opening diversity, stratified by rating and game volume."
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-pos: H
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-width: 7


div_strata <- dbGetQuery(con, sprintf("
  WITH x AS (
    SELECT player, month, opening_diversity, games, avg_rating
    FROM read_parquet(%s)
    WHERE opening_diversity IS NOT NULL
      AND games IS NOT NULL
      AND avg_rating IS NOT NULL
  ),
  y AS (
    SELECT *,
      LEAD(avg_rating) OVER (PARTITION BY player ORDER BY month) AS next_rating
    FROM x
  ),
  z AS (
    SELECT
      CAST(FLOOR(avg_rating/200)*200 AS INTEGER) AS rating_bin,
      CASE
        WHEN games < 10 THEN '<10'
        WHEN games < 25 THEN '10–24'
        WHEN games < 60 THEN '25–59'
        ELSE '60+'
      END AS games_bin,
      opening_diversity,
      (next_rating - avg_rating) AS d_rating_next
    FROM y
    WHERE next_rating IS NOT NULL
  )
  SELECT
    rating_bin,
    games_bin,
    opening_diversity,
    AVG(d_rating_next) AS mean_d,
    COUNT(*) AS n
  FROM z
  GROUP BY rating_bin, games_bin, opening_diversity
  HAVING n >= 5
  ORDER BY rating_bin, games_bin, opening_diversity
", qpath(paths$pm)))

div_strata <- div_strata |>
  mutate(games_bin = factor(games_bin, levels = c("60+", "25–59", "10–24", "<10")))

ggplot(div_strata, aes(x=opening_diversity, y=mean_d, color=games_bin)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~rating_bin, scales="free_y") +
  labs(x = "Opening Diversity (Within-Month)", y = "Mean Next-Month Rating Change",
       color="Games") +
  scale_color_few() +
  theme_few() + 
  theme(
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(linewidth = 0.3, colour = "grey85"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )

```
